title: Post-processing landscapes from Painted Desert trip: single-zone to multi-zone, panorama, and color-work

locations.name: Painted Desert (explicit in video title)
locations.basis: Video title and opening narration reference Painted Desert Trip 3

locations.name: Henry Mountains
locations.basis: Explicit mention: “the Henry Mountains… from here” at ~00:04:05

summary: This video documents a practical, on-location post-processing workflow for landscape and abstract shots, starting with single-zone images and moving through compositional cropping, tonal adjustments, selective color and color grading, and then advancing to multi-zone processing, dodge/burn, and sky/foreground separation. It includes a hands-on panorama workflow (using PTGui) and a variety of Photoshop/Lightroom techniques (histories, clone-paint, gradient-based edits, and wide-angle filter effects) to emphasize directional light, depth, and layered composition. The presenter emphasizes non-destructive editing, scene-by-scene decisions, and the difference between processing a one-zone shot versus a three-zone (or more) composition, with concrete examples from desert canyon locations.
topics: color grading tool and multiple passes
clone stamp and history brush (non-destructive edits)
drone twilight habits and exposure-to-the-right principle
leading lines and rule-of-six in landscape planning
layer separation to create depth (level of blacks)
color grading hierarchies and tonal adjustments
post-processing order and non-destructive rollback workflows
exposure compensation and clipped highlights handling

sections.title: Overview: from single-zone images to post-processing plan
sections.description: The host frames the trip as a set of single-zone images with minimal post-processing, then pivots to techniques like panorama stitching and basic tonal tweaks. He distinguishes one-zone images (which can be processed quickly) from multi-zone scenes requiring more careful blending and directional lighting.

sections.title: Cropping strategy and rule-of-six composition
sections.description: Demonstrates cropping to remove empty space, positioning mountains as a third of the frame, and ensuring six zones contain something of interest. Emphasizes starting/ending crops early, and using focal length to achieve the desired thirds composition.

sections.title: Directional light and initial tonal refinements
sections.description: Shows how to bias light toward the side where illumination comes from, using the burn tool to emphasize peaks, then applying a whites-dominant contrast step that preserves sky quality while enhancing foreground.

sections.title: Selective color, sky treatment, and color grading passes
sections.description: Introduces selective color to fix specific ridges, then strong, staged color grading for both sky and land, including using the history brush to apply precise adjustments to selected regions. Highlights the need to adjust color temperature/tint before applying color grading for a natural look.

sections.title: Twilight and multiple-zone processing concepts (Fisher Towers and more)
sections.description: Discusses twilight shots, the challenges of underexposure, and introduces multi-zone processing to manage foreground, towers, and sky separately. Illustrates how to dodge/burn and selectively color the different zones to achieve depth and directional lighting, with emphasis on maintaining consistency across zones.

sections.title: Panorama creation workflow and multi-shot stitching
sections.description: Walks through selecting multiple frames, loading into PTGui, stitching into a panorama, and recommending rectilinear distortion for landscape panoramas. Emphasizes saving intermediate layers and maintaining non-destructive workflow while assembling a multi-shot panorama.

sections.title: Post-stitch processing and ongoing refinement
sections.description: Covers post-stitch refinements: tone-mapping, selective color, and color grading to harmonize the panorama, plus considerations for cropping the final composition to foregrounds with layered depth.
